newsitem.title: BELARUS: Lukashenko attacks critics on Belarus union.
newsitem.headline: Lukashenko attacks critics on Belarus union.

text.p: Hardline President Alexander Lukashenko, due to seal the union of Belarus with Russia in four days, on Monday took a swipe at critics in Moscow who fear he will use it to boost his influence in the Kremlin.

Lukashenko did not refer directly to liberals in Moscow who are reported to be trying to scale down the powers of a joint council which will govern the union, but said President Boris Yeltsin was coming under undue pressure.
"Those who want to reduce the functions of the international organ are profoundly mistaken," he told reporters as he stood beside his helicopter after visiting the eastern village of Dribin.

Asked about Yeltsin's position on the charter, which the two men are due to sign in Moscow on May 23, Lukashenko said: "You see what pressure is on him. I have no idea how he keeps it up. Perhaps he has already stopped studying mass media and does not watch television or read newspapers."
He seemed to be referring to what he sees as a Russian media campaign against his rule, which has grown increasingly authoritarian and faced harsh criticism in the West.

Lukashenko said drafts of the charter had been delivered to both presidents and three issues had still to be resolved -- the authority of the organ governing the union, what powers its leader will have and its location -- apparently Minsk or Moscow.
Yeltsin has said a complete merger of the two countries would be the ultimate goal of the charter -- an idea opposed by Lukashenko who wants a union of two sovereign states.

While Russia has a population of 150 million and is keeping international lending bodies satisfied as it pushes ahead with reforms, Belarus and its 10 million people have had their credit programmes suspended pending faster reforms.
Belarussian, a Slav tongue close to Polish and Russian, is used by a small minority in daily life though it is used alongside Russian on both state television channels and radio.
The country's identity has been all but crushed by centuries of foreign rule and it has no modern history as an independent state.
Lukashenko's critics in Moscow reportedly persuaded Yeltsin to sign a skeleton treaty on April 2, setting aside much of the proposed union to be signed later.
Lukashenko had been seeking a supranational body with powers to make decisions about the union but he said on Monday the latest draft foresaw at best an international body.
The two presidents are due to meet on Thursday on the eve of the document's signing to settle outstanding issues.
